name: Java
title: Java (Java 27)

presenceList.meta: R2, R3, Ec6, Ec7, V5, D3, L2, Q4

preamble.text: Analysis against Java 27 (general availability, 15 September 2026, JSR 402). Java 27 is a runtime release: it finalises no language feature and adds no new language construct, so every scored mechanism holds the value it held for Java 26 and the score is identical. What the release changes is what the virtual machine does by default — the collector, the object header, the TLS key exchange, the Flight Recorder output — and this page records each of those where it bears on a dimension.

type.text: **Interfaces decouple specification from implementation**: Can program to interfaces
**Generics enable type parameterization**: `List<T>` decouples from concrete types
**Sealed classes (Java 17)**: Controlled inheritance hierarchies — the class author decides which subclasses exist, decoupling from unknown extensions
**Records (Java 16)**: Immutable data carriers with auto-generated `equals`/`hashCode`/`toString` — construction decoupled from mutation
**Pattern matching (Java 21)**: `switch` expressions + sealed types enable exhaustive, compositional dispatch

**Primitive types in patterns, fifth preview (Java 27)**: `instanceof` and `switch` accept `int`, `long`, `double`, and the rest in type patterns, so a `switch` over a numeric domain narrows with a checked conversion instead of a hand-written cast. Re-previewed unchanged from Java 26 (JEP 532), so the construct needs `--enable-preview`
**No higher-kinded types**: Can't abstract over generic types
**Type erasure couples generics**: Runtime loses type information, so a consumer recovers the type argument at a cast site the compiler cannot check
**Inheritance still available**: Unchecked class extension possible (unless `final` or `sealed`)
**Null still exists**: `NullPointerException` possible (no non-nullable types in the language)

**Module system (Java 9+) limits reflection**: Strong encapsulation of non-exported packages became the default in Java 16, so reflective access to them now needs an explicit `--add-opens` — reflection is no longer a free-for-all
**Package-private couples to package structure**: Visibility tied to organization
char is a UTF-16 code unit and String.length counts units (JLS); code-point APIs are the opt-in

construction.text: **Records are immutable by default**: `record Point(int x, int y)` — no mutation coupling, auto-generated components
**Copy-with-change without mutation**: Records have no withers or copy constructors, so a copy-with-change is a hand-written call that supplies the new value and copies the rest

**Lazy constants, third preview (Java 27)**: `LazyConstant` holds an unmodifiable value computed once, on first use, and the JVM optimises it as a constant in the way `final` allows — the single-checked-locking idiom and its hand-written publication ordering are no longer the programmer's job (JEP 531). Preview API
**Dependency injection frameworks**: Spring/Guice decouple construction from usage
**Records eliminate builders for simple cases**: Complex multi-step construction may still need builders
**Constructors couple creation to initialization**: Not eliminated, but records and patterns reduce the problem
**Static methods couple to global state**: Singleton pattern creates hidden dependencies
**Collection order is unpinned**: HashMap iterates in a hash-dependent order the specification does not fix, and the ordered map is the opt-in a disciplined team must choose
**One value, many names**: every object is reached through references, an array's buffer is shared by assignment, and no declaration names the alias set — a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type
Class initialization is first-touch; JLS 12.4.1 documents the cycle: a thread observes zero fields, and a cycle can deadlock

memory.text: **JVM GC decouples memory**: Modern GCs (ZGC, Generational ZGC, Shenandoah) provide sub-millisecond pause times

**G1 is the default collector in every environment (Java 27)**: The JVM no longer falls back to Serial on a small machine, so one collector governs a one-CPU container and a large server alike (JEP 523). A deployment that measured better with Serial still selects it explicitly

**Compact object headers by default (Java 27)**: The object header shrinks from 96 bits to 64 on 64-bit architectures, so the same object graph fits in less heap — 22% less on SPECjbb2015 in the JEP's measurement (JEP 534). `-XX:-UseCompactObjectHeaders` restores the old layout
**No manual memory management**: Can't have dangling pointers
**Foreign Function & Memory API (Java 22)**: Safe memory access without JNI, decoupling native interop from unsafety

**Ahead-of-time object caching (Java 26)**: Startup work moves into a cached archive instead of being repeated per process; Java 27 adds `-XX:AOTMode=required` as the spelling to use in place of `-XX:AOTMode=on`, which is to be deprecated and removed
**GC pauses affect latency**: Minimized by modern GCs but not deterministic
**Memory leaks from static references**: Static collections couple to application lifetime (still possible)

error.text: **Checked exceptions separate error paths**: `throws IOException` makes errors explicit
**Pattern matching for `switch` + sealed types (Java 21)**: Exhaustive error handling — compiler verifies all error cases covered
**Primitive types in patterns (fifth preview, Java 27)**: Exhaustive switching over numeric domains, with the narrowing conversion checked rather than written by hand

**Structured concurrency reports a failed subtask as one outcome (seventh preview, Java 27)**: `join()` throws the exception its `Joiner` produces, and the new third type parameter names that exception, so the failure of a subtree arrives in one place instead of as a flag each subtask sets (JEP 533)
**Try-catch doesn't compose**: Can't map/flatMap over exceptions without wrapping
**RuntimeException bypasses checks**: Unchecked exceptions defer error-coupling detection to runtime (sealed hierarchies with pattern matching help)

concurrency.text: **Virtual threads (stable, Java 21+)**: Lightweight threads — each task gets its own thread, eliminating callback coupling

**Structured concurrency (seventh preview, Java 27)**: `StructuredTaskScope` scopes subtask lifetimes to a lexical block; the seventh round adds a type parameter for the exception `join()` may throw and an `open` factory that applies a configuration to the default join policy (JEP 533). Preview API, so production code cannot rely on the shape it has today

**A task scope is a block**: `ExecutorService` is `AutoCloseable`, and `close()` waits until every task submitted to it has completed, so a try-with-resources block joins the work it launched; the richer `StructuredTaskScope` is still a preview
**Scoped values (final, Java 25+)**: Thread-local data with guaranteed cleanup, decoupling context from global state
**Shared mutable state still possible**: `synchronized`, `volatile`, and manual lock patterns remain available

platform.text: **Open specifications**: The Java Language Specification and the JVM Specification are public standards that any conforming implementation may implement — Java 27 is the reference implementation of Java SE 27 (JSR 402)
**Multiple vendor runtimes**: OpenJDK, Oracle JDK, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, and GraalVM run the same class files
**Open-source core**: OpenJDK is developed in the open under the GPL with the Classpath Exception
**Portable bytecode**: Compiled classes run unchanged on every platform that hosts a JVM

performance.text: **Virtual threads**: Low-overhead concurrency scales to millions of threads

**One collector to reason about (Java 27)**: G1 is the default everywhere, and the synchronization work that landed in Java 26 brought its throughput close to Serial's on constrained machines (JEP 523)

**Less heap per object graph (Java 27)**: Compact object headers are on by default — 8% less CPU time and 15% fewer collections on SPECjbb2015 in the JEP's measurements, and about 10% less time on a parallel JSON parser (JEP 534)

**Faster post-quantum and Curve25519 arithmetic (Java 27)**: SHA-3 intrinsics for AVX-512 lift ML-KEM by 46–48% and ML-DSA by 38–74%; optimised Curve25519 field operations lift X25519 and Ed25519 by roughly 46–55% on x86-64 and AArch64
**GC pauses**: Tunable; ZGC offers sub-millisecond pauses
**Startup time**: JIT warmup (mitigated by ahead-of-time object caching, GraalVM native image, CDS archives, and CRaC)

ecosystem.text: **Enterprise monoculture**: Spring dominates the server stack, so the alternatives are not really alternatives

**Legacy burden**: The enterprise stack keeps a 1999-era API in service next to a 2027 one, so a library supports both — Java 27 retires `ThreadPoolExecutor.finalize()` and four discontinued launcher options while the older APIs they sit beside remain

**One fewer runtime configuration (Java 27)**: The JVM Compiler Interface and `-XX:+UseGraalJIT` were removed, so a stock JDK no longer accepts a substitute compiler; a team that chose its JDK for a different JIT must now choose a distribution that ships one
The class file carries a published promise across JDK releases [@javaJLS]

evolution.text: **Regular releases**: 6-month cadence, LTS every 2 years. Java 27 is a feature release, not an LTS: the long-term line is Java 25, so a production deployment that must stay on an LTS waits
**Preview features**: Opt-in features decouple experimentation from production stability

**Deprecation reaches removal (Java 27)**: `ThreadPoolExecutor.finalize()` — deprecated for removal since Java 18 — is gone, as are `-noclassgc`, `-noverify`, `-verifyremote`, and `-Xverify:none`. The cycle that marks an API obsolete and then deletes it now completes within a few releases
**Legacy burden**: Old APIs accumulate (though the deprecated-for-removal process is active; the applet API went in Java 26)

**Two defaults moved with no compiler error (Java 27)**: ML-KEM and ML-DSA private keys now encode as a `seed` rather than an expanded key, so a key this JDK writes cannot be read by an older release unless `jdk.mlkem.pkcs8.encoding` is set before the key is made, and `KeyFactory.translateKey` converts an existing key to the old form. G1 also replaced the Serial selection on small machines, so a deployment that never named a collector now runs a different one; `-XX:+UseSerialGC` restores the old choice. Both changes are recorded and neither is priced: the `seed` form is better interoperability by RFC 9935, and G1 everywhere is faster on constrained machines by the JEP's own measurements — so the same presence would have to mean a gain and a loss at once, and a cost with no fixed direction cannot enter a sum that is compared across languages

**`final` fields still only warn (Java 27)**: Deep reflection that mutates a `final` field reports the warning introduced in Java 26; the release that blocks such mutation by default has not arrived, so an ecosystem that depends on it has no deadline yet

**Flags drift out of date without the code changing**: `-XX:UseCompressedClassPointers` became obsolete in Java 27 and is ignored with a warning, and `-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent` is renamed `-XX:G1IHOP` with the old name kept as a deprecated alias

domain.text: **Long-lived network services (Java 27)**: Post-quantum hybrid key exchange heads the default TLS 1.3 group list, so a service on `javax.net.ssl` gets harvest-now-decrypt-later protection without a code change (JEP 527)
**Poor for frontend**: Applet API removed (Java 26); JavaFX remains niche

learning.text: **Modern Java is growing in surface**: Records, sealed types, pattern matching, virtual threads, modules — more to learn than Java 8
**Legacy/Modern split**: Learning the "right" modern way requires guidance

**Preview churn dates the tutorials (Java 27)**: Structured concurrency has been in preview since Java 21 and changed shape again in Java 27; primitive types in patterns have been in preview since Java 23 and changed in Java 26. A tutorial written against an earlier release may not compile against this one

syntax.text: **Records eliminate getter/setter boilerplate**: `record Person(String name, int age)` replaces 50-line POJO
**Pattern matching reduces verbosity**: `switch` expressions + sealed types
**Still verbose compared to Kotlin/Scala**: Type erasure, generics syntax

testing.text: **Excellent debuggers**: Step-through, breakpoints, virtual thread debugging

**Flight Recorder redacts secrets before they leave the process (Java 27)**: Command-line arguments, initial environment variables, and initial system properties are filtered in-process, so a recording can be attached to a support case; `-XX:FlightRecorderOptions:redact-key` and `redact-argument` extend the filter (JEP 536)

**Diagnostics reach the shell and the crash log (Java 27)**: `jcmd` gains a Bash completion script and a `VM.security_properties` command, and `VM.info` and the `hs_err_pid` log report the open file-descriptor count

security.text: **Module system**: Restricts reflective access to non-exported packages by default (Java 16+)

**Post-quantum hybrid key exchange by default (Java 27)**: `X25519MLKEM768` heads the default named-group list, combining ML-KEM-768 with X25519 so that a session stays secure while either half survives; `SecP256r1MLKEM768` and `SecP384r1MLKEM1024` are available on request (JEP 527)
**TLS certificate compression (Java 27)**: zlib compression of certificate chains is on by default, shrinking the handshake
**PEM API (third preview, Java 27)**: Encodes and decodes keys, certificates, and revocation lists in the transport format every other toolchain already reads (JEP 538)
**Serialization vulnerabilities**: Deserialization attacks (mitigated by records + modern serialization frameworks)
Integer arithmetic is two's-complement wraparound by specification (JLS 15.7.2), silent in a shipped build

reproducibility.text: **No contract the toolchain reads**: the JDK compiler consumes the command line, and the dependency contract lives in third-party build tooling the platform does not ship

supplychain.text: The JDK ships no package channel: jars move through Maven Central, a third-party repository whose terms are its own.

observability.text: JDK Flight Recorder ships a stable recording standard for latency, allocation, and method sampling in the JVM itself.
The runtime writes hs_err_pid files, thread dumps, and heap dumps by default, so a crash carries its own post-mortem.

interop.text: JNI is the in-process foreign interface, and the Foreign Function and Memory API modernizes it.
The JVM is the portable target: the artifact runs wherever a compatible JVM runs.

governance.text: The Java Community Process runs the language evolution through public JSRs and expert groups.
The Java Language Specification is published and complete.
The JCK conformance kit runs against every licensed implementation.
javac and the JDK libraries are public source in OpenJDK.

feedback.text: javac compiles the edit-run loop in seconds.
Editor analysis rides the javac API, so IDE diagnostics match the compiler.

tradeoffs: **Checked exceptions vs. composition**: Explicit errors don't compose natively (no monadic operations), though sealed types + pattern matching provide exhaustive error handling

**Backward compatibility vs. modern features**: 30 years of legacy — old codebases can lag behind modern idioms, and the removals now arrive: the JVM Compiler Interface, `ThreadPoolExecutor.finalize()`, and four launcher options all went in Java 27
**Null as default vs. safety**: Everything nullable by default couples all code to defensive checks — records and pattern matching help but don't solve the root issue
**Type erasure vs. runtime types**: Generics erased at runtime couples generic code to raw types
**Inheritance vs. composition**: Hierarchy coupling possible when teams choose extension over composition

**Preview features vs. availability**: Two of the best new constructs — primitive types in patterns, five previews old, and the `StructuredTaskScope` API, seven — still need `--enable-preview`, so the language's own guidance is that production code waits for the richer form and joins tasks through a block-scoped `ExecutorService` instead. A feature that stays preview is a feature most codebases cannot use

**Default changes vs. predictability**: Java 27 changes what the JVM does with no code change: a different collector on small machines, a different header layout, a different default ML-KEM private-key encoding that older releases cannot read. A deployment that measured its way to the old defaults must now opt out of the new ones
verdict: Java 27 spends the release on the runtime, not the language, and the score says so: not one scored mechanism moves, because a default collector, a header width, and a cipher suite are not constructs the compiler accepts or rejects. What the language gives — records, sealed types, exhaustive pattern matching, virtual threads, modules — is Java 26's, and what it charges — null in every reference, erased generics, unchecked failures in practice, an unproven locking discipline, a Spring-shaped ecosystem — is Java 26's as well. The release earns its place on defaults that used to be advice: G1 is the collector everywhere, so one tuning story covers a laptop and a server (JEP 523); object headers are 64 bits, so the same object graph occupies less heap and less memory bandwidth (JEP 534); TLS 1.3 prefers a hybrid post-quantum key exchange, so harvest-now-decrypt-later stops being a migration project (JEP 527); Flight Recorder redacts secrets before a recording leaves the process (JEP 536). It also removes, and one removal matters: the JVM Compiler Interface and `-XX:+UseGraalJIT` are gone, so a stock JDK no longer accepts a substitute compiler, and the compiler a distribution ships is the compiler you have. Main strength: the platform's defaults now express its best practice, without a code change. Main weakness: unchanged — null, erasure, and a preview pipeline whose two flagship features are five and seven rounds old.
verdictExtra: > **Note:** The score reflects modern Java idioms: records over POJOs, sealed types over open hierarchies, virtual threads over thread pools, pattern matching over `instanceof` chains.

> **Note:** No scored mechanism differs from Java 26. Java 27 finalises no language feature, so the inventory prices the same language twice; the two pages differ in what the runtime now does by default and in what was removed, which the observations record and the score does not. A coupling score is a property of the language the compiler accepts.

energy.text: Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [@joel2025lowresource; @effibenchx2025].

safety.text: A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

delivery.note: The class-file format and the binary compatibility rules are published by the JVM specification
